title: Mary Coyle first speaks in the Moot
summary: Mary Coyle, widowed of the Cuan bheag drowning, stands and speaks her own words in the Moot at Caol mhòr rather than sending a note forward to be read by another. The clerk David Hale sets her speech down whole in the day-book, the first time a woman's words are kept there entire rather than summed in a line.

title: The widows heard first
summary: The Moot resolves that the widows of the drowned be heard on the same footing as any man who has paid his shilling, and heard first when a matter touches their own dead. The rule is entered as standing, not as a courtesy for one night, on the widow Agnes Tulloch's motion.

title: The Hawk's twentieth first paid
summary: Ros gheal's factor pays the Hawk houses their first quarter's twentieth on the dues of the new grain dock, the sum the shire's factor haggled down from a tithe. The due is paid every quarter after, and the clerks of Ros gheal come to call it simply the Hawk's, few remembering why.

title: The Moot votes to send the western crossing
summary: After two hard sittings the Moot agrees to Mary Coyle's asking, that northern boats sail west-about to keep the sea-feast at Seann Bhral where the Tuathaich forebears once kept it. Many in the room call it a fool's errand for winter, and are not silenced, only outvoted.

title: Eleven boats sail for Seann Bhral
summary: Eleven boats out of Caol mhòr, Cuan bheag and Ros mhòr put out on a grey morning at the end of an Lùnastal under Mary Coyle, carrying little but themselves, a keg of salt fish apiece, and the Moot's own sheet naming her their word. Ros bheag's harbour will not give them its quay, and sends them to a mooring buoy instead.

title: A boat nearly lost off the passage
summary: A squall out of the south-west puts green water over the bow of the smallest boat of the eleven, and its crew bails her clear with whatever will hold water. No one of the fleet is lost on the four days' passage, though more than one aboard call it the hardest going since the Crossing itself.

title: The house at Seann Bhral answers Mary Coyle
summary: The keeper of Manannan's order at Seann Bhral in the west hears Mary Coyle's asking through to the end and refuses it: the house is kept on tithes of families who hold the rite by blood and the custodian's book, and cannot be opened on a four days' claim, however justly sailed. He tells her the sea is the same; the house is not.

title: Mary Coyle resolves to keep the feast at Cnoc ghorm
summary: On the passage home Mary Coyle tells the crews the north will keep the feast of the sea itself, in full, at the church above Cnoc ghorm where a thin blessing of the boats is already kept each spring. The decision is made before the eleven boats raise Caol mhòr again.

title: The first Fleadh na Mara kept in full
summary: More than fifty boats gather at Cnoc ghorm on the second Sunday of an Gearran, far beyond any year before, and the parish priest blesses each hull in turn with heather dipped in harbour water. Mary Coyle's own boat, which carried her to Seann Bhral and back, is blessed fourth in the row.

title: David Hale counts the boats at Cnoc ghorm
summary: David Hale keeps a written count of the boats blessed at Cnoc ghorm for the Moot's day-book, the first such count taken of the feast. Word of the gathering's size travels the north coast faster than the crossing to Seann Bhral had, and boats are promised from as far as Inis mhin's country the year after.

title: A Ros mhòr man asks what now
summary: On the third day home from Seann Bhral, off the northern capes, an old Ros mhòr hand who has said little the whole voyage asks Mary Coyle plainly what she means to do now that the west will not have them.
